description: Falconry among the nomadic peoples of the Eurasian steppe developed as both a practical hunting method and a marker of prestige. Mounted hunters trained falcons, hawks, and in some regions eagles to pursue hares, foxes, birds, and other game across open grasslands where visibility and mobility favored hunting with raptors. The practice fit naturally with steppe horse culture, combining skilled riding, animal husbandry, and close knowledge of seasonal landscapes. Over time, falconry also became associated with elite status, diplomacy, and ceremonial display among many Turkic, Mongolic, and Iranian-speaking steppe societies.
